from _stats import (describe, five_number_summary, shape_report,

                    quartiles, iqr, outlier_fences,
                    z_score, z_scores, coefficient_of_variation,

                    grouped_mean, grouped_variance, grouped_summary,

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

def money(x, decimals=0):
    return f"${x:,.{decimals}f}"


def num(x, decimals=0):
    return f"{x:,.{decimals}f}"


def mnum(x, decimals=0):
    """A number formatted for the inside of a LaTeX expression.

    Thousands separators have to be written {,} in math mode, and a bare
    dollar sign would close the equation. Both are handled here so the
    displayed formula reads the way it would be written on a whiteboard.
    """
    return f"{x:,.{decimals}f}".replace(",", "{,}")


def mmoney(x, decimals=0):
    return r"\$" + mnum(x, decimals)


def show_math(latex):
    """Print a display equation. Used from chunks marked `output: asis`, so
    that computed values reach LaTeX without being escaped on the way."""
    print(f"$${latex}$$\n")


states  = pd.read_csv("data/state_hpi_ur_pop.csv")

# Measures of Central Tendency

::: {.blue}
**Central tendency** is a single value used to describe a central focal point
in a data set.
:::

## The Mean

::: {.blue}
Given a data series $X=\{x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n\}$, the sample **mean** is

$$\bar{x}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i,$$

where $n$ is the number of members of the sample. For a population we write

$$\mu=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}x_i,$$

where $N$ is the number of members of the population.
:::

The mean is easy to compute, easy to explain, and always produces exactly one
number. That is its entire case for the defence. Here is the case against.

### Example: the population of the Western states

```{python}
#| label: west-table
west_sorted = west.sort_values("People")[["Member", "People"]]
west_sorted.assign(People=west_sorted["People"].map(lambda v: f"{v:,.0f}")) \
           .reset_index(drop=True)
```

```{python}
#| label: west-stats
#| include: false

w_mean = west["People"].mean()
w_median = west["People"].median()
w_above = int((west["People"] > w_mean).sum())
w_below = int((west["People"] < w_mean).sum())
w_asof = pd.to_datetime(pops["as_of"]).max().date()
```

The mean population of a Western state is `{python} num(w_mean)`, as of
`{python} str(w_asof)`. But only `{python} str(w_above)` of the
`{python} str(len(west))` Western states have a population larger than that
mean, and `{python} str(w_below)` have a smaller one.

::: {.scarlet}
A "central" value that `{python} str(w_below)` of `{python} str(len(west))`
observations fall below is not describing a centre. It is describing
California.
:::

```{python}
#| label: west-charts
_ = box_plot(west["People"], title="Population of the Western states",
             xlab="People")
```

```{python}
#| label: west-hist
_ = histogram(west["People"], bins=6,
              title="Population of the Western states",
              xlab="People", ylab="Number of states")
```

::: {.blue}
**Outliers** are values much higher or lower than most of the data. The mean
is pulled toward them. The median is not.
:::

## The Weighted Mean

::: {.blue}
For a data set $\{x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n\}$ with corresponding weights
$\{w_1,w_2,\dots,w_n\}$, the **weighted mean** is

$$\bar{x}_w=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_ix_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_i}.$$
:::

This is the formula MBAs get wrong most often in practice, usually by not
reaching for it at all. Consider the unemployment rate of the fifty states.

```{python}
#| label: weighted-unemployment
plain = states["UR"].mean()
weighted = (states["UR"] * states["POPN"]).sum() / states["POPN"].sum()

pd.DataFrame({
    "measure": ["Unweighted mean of the 50 state rates",
                "Population-weighted mean"],
    "unemployment rate (%)": [round(plain, 2), round(weighted, 2)],
})
```

```{python}
#| label: weighted-detail
#| include: false

biggest = states.nlargest(1, "POPN").iloc[0]
smallest = states.nsmallest(1, "POPN").iloc[0]
ur_asof = pd.to_datetime(states["UR_date"]).max().date()
gap = weighted - plain
```

The two answers differ by `{python} f"{gap:+.2f}"` percentage points, and only
one of them is the unemployment rate of the country. The unweighted mean gives
`{python} smallest["Member"]` — population
`{python} num(smallest["POPN"] * 1000)` — exactly the same say as
`{python} biggest["Member"]`, population
`{python} num(biggest["POPN"] * 1000)`.

::: {.charcoal}
Whenever the things you are averaging represent groups of different sizes —
states, stores, regions, customer segments — the plain average answers the
question *"what is the typical store's rate?"* and the weighted average
answers *"what is the rate across all customers?"* Those are different
questions. Decide which one you were asked before you pick a formula.
:::

## The Median

::: {.blue}
The **median** is the value for which half the observations are higher and
half are lower.

The **index point** is the position of the median once the data are arranged
in ascending order:

$$i=0.5\,n,$$

where $n$ is the number of observations. If $i$ is not an integer, round up
and take the value in that position. If $i$ is an integer, take the average of
the values in positions $i$ and $i+1$.
:::

### The Western states again

```{python}
#| label: west-median
#| include: false

w_diff = w_mean - w_median
```

The median population of a Western state is `{python} num(w_median)`. The
mean is `{python} num(w_mean)` — higher by `{python} num(w_diff)`.

The list is already sorted above. With $n=`{python} str(len(west))`$, the index
point is $0.5 \times `{python} str(len(west))` = `{python} f"{0.5*len(west):g}"`$,
which is not an integer, so we round up to position
`{python} str(int(np.ceil(0.5*len(west))))` and read off the value there.

### An even number of observations

New England has six states, so the index point lands exactly on an integer and
the second half of the rule applies.

```{python}
#| label: ne-table
ne_sorted = newengland.sort_values("People")[["Member", "People"]].reset_index(drop=True)
ne_sorted.assign(position=range(1, len(ne_sorted) + 1),
                 People=ne_sorted["People"].map(lambda v: f"{v:,.0f}"))
```

```{python}
#| label: ne-stats
#| include: false

ne_vals = newengland["People"].sort_values().to_numpy()
ne3, ne4 = ne_vals[2], ne_vals[3]
ne_median = 0.5 * (ne3 + ne4)
ne_mean = newengland["People"].mean()
```

With $n=6$, the index point is $0.5 \times 6 = 3$. Three is an integer, so the
median is the average of the third and fourth values:

```{python}
#| label: ne-median-math
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
show_math(rf"\frac{{1}}{{2}}\left({mnum(ne3)} + {mnum(ne4)}\right)"
          rf" = {mnum(ne_median)}")
```

The mean is `{python} num(ne_mean)` and the median is
`{python} num(ne_median)`, a difference of
`{python} num(ne_mean - ne_median)`. Compare that to the
`{python} num(w_diff)` gap out West. Same statistic, same country, a far
smaller disagreement — because New England has no California in it.

## The Mode

::: {.blue}
The **mode** is the value that appears most often in a data set. It is the
only measure of central tendency that works on categories.
:::

### Example: US patents granted, by country of origin

```{python}
#| label: patents-table
countries = [c for c in patents.columns if c != "date"]
recent = patents.dropna(subset=countries).iloc[-1]
patents.assign(year=patents["date"].dt.year) \
       .set_index("year")[countries].tail(12) \
       .style.format("{:,.0f}")
```

```{python}
#| label: patents-bar
latest = recent[countries].astype(float)
_ = bar_chart(latest.index, latest.to_numpy(),
              title=f"Patents granted in {recent['date'].year}, by country of origin",
              xlab="Country of origin", ylab="Patents granted")
```

```{python}
#| label: patents-stats
#| include: false

mode_country = latest.idxmax()
mode_share = 100 * latest.max() / latest.sum()
pat_last_year = recent["date"].year
pat_first_year = patents["date"].dt.year.min()
```

The modal country of origin is `{python} mode_country`, with
`{python} num(latest.max())` patents — `{python} f"{mode_share:.1f}"`% of the
five countries shown.

::: {.scarlet}
This series runs from `{python} str(pat_first_year)` through
`{python} str(pat_last_year)`. It is not current, and the FRED page it comes
from does not put a banner on the chart telling you so. Chapter 2 asked you to
check the last observation date of every series you use. This is the series
that punishes you for skipping that step.
:::

Notice also that a mean of these five numbers would be a nonsense statistic —
the average of the US, China, Japan, Germany and the UK is not a country. When
your variable is a category, the mode is the only measure of central tendency
available to you.

# The Shapes of Distributions

::: {.brown}
A **symmetrical** distribution is a mirror image about its centre. Its mean
and median are approximately equal.

In a **left-skewed** distribution, the median is larger than the mean.

In a **right-skewed** distribution, the median is smaller than the mean.
:::

The single most useful diagnostic in this chapter is free: compute the mean
and the median and compare them. If they are far apart, one of them is lying
to you about the middle.

## Approximately symmetric: the US unemployment rate

```{python}
#| label: unrate-hist
_ = histogram(unrate["unemployment_rate"], bins=20,
              title="US unemployment rate, monthly",
              xlab="Unemployment rate (%)", ylab="Months")
```

```{python}
#| label: unrate-summary
describe(unrate["unemployment_rate"], name="UNRATE").to_frame()
```

::: {.brown}
Watch the `mode` row across this chapter. It carries a value here only because
FRED publishes the unemployment rate rounded to one decimal place, so months
tie by accident of rounding rather than because the economy has a favourite
number. On an unrounded measurement — the return series later in this chapter
— the same row reads `NaN`, because no value repeats and there is no mode to
report. That blank is the honest answer. The mode earns its keep on
categories, as it did with the patent data above, and rarely anywhere else.
:::

```{python}
#| label: unrate-box
_ = box_plot(unrate["unemployment_rate"],
             title="US unemployment rate, monthly",
             xlab="Unemployment rate (%)")
```

```{python}
#| label: unrate-shape
print(shape_report(unrate["unemployment_rate"], "US unemployment rate"))
print(f"Coverage: {unrate['date'].min():%B %Y} to {unrate['date'].max():%B %Y}"
      f"  ({len(unrate):,} months)")
```

```{python}
#| label: unrate-stats
#| include: false

u_mean = unrate["unemployment_rate"].mean()
u_median = unrate["unemployment_rate"].median()
u_gap = u_mean - u_median
u_sd = unrate["unemployment_rate"].std(ddof=1)
u_gap_in_sd = abs(u_gap) / u_sd
u_side = "above" if u_gap > 0 else "below"
u_tail = "right" if u_gap > 0 else "left"
```

The mean is `{python} f"{u_mean:.2f}"` and the median is
`{python} f"{u_median:.2f}"` — a gap of `{python} f"{u_gap:+.2f}"` percentage
points, which is `{python} f"{u_gap_in_sd:.2f}"` of a standard deviation. That
is what approximate symmetry looks like in numbers rather than in a picture:
not identical, but close enough that either one would serve as "the typical
month."

In this series the mean sits slightly `{python} u_side` the median, which
makes the `{python} u_tail` tail marginally the longer one — but a gap that
small is not a finding, and it can change sign as more months are added.

What is not in doubt is the mechanism. Unemployment rises hard and fast in a
recession and comes back down slowly, so the months far from the centre tend
to be the high ones, and the box plot shows those sitting past the upper
fence. Compare that to the GPA and income distributions below, where the gap
between mean and median is large enough to survive any amount of new data.

## Left-skewed: graduate student GPA

```{python}
#| label: gpa-hist
_ = histogram(gpa["GPA"], bins=20,
              title="Graduate student GPA",
              xlab="GPA", ylab="Number of students")
```

```{python}
#| label: gpa-shape
print(shape_report(gpa["GPA"], "Graduate GPA"))
```

```{python}
#| label: gpa-summary
describe(gpa["GPA"], name="GPA").to_frame()
```

The median exceeds the mean, which is the definition of left skew. The cause
is visible in the histogram: GPA has a hard ceiling at 4.0 and no floor to
speak of, so the only direction an unusual student can be unusual *in* is
downward. A few very low GPAs drag the mean below the median while the bulk of
the distribution piles up against the ceiling.

::: {.charcoal}
Any measure with a ceiling tends to skew left: exam scores, on-time delivery
rates, satisfaction surveys capped at 5. Any measure with a floor at zero and
no ceiling tends to skew right: income, insurance claims, time on hold,
company size. Knowing which one you are holding tells you what to expect
before you compute anything.
:::

## Right-skewed: Nevada adjusted gross income

```{python}
#| label: agi-hist
_ = histogram(agi["AGI"], bins=40,
              title="Nevada household adjusted gross income, 2016",
              xlab="AGI ($10,000s)", ylab="Households")
```

```{python}
#| label: agi-shape
print(shape_report(agi["AGI"], "Nevada AGI ($10,000s)"))
print(f"n = {len(agi):,} households in this sample")
```

```{python}
#| label: agi-summary
describe(agi["AGI"], name="AGI ($10,000s)").to_frame()
```

```{python}
#| label: agi-stats
#| include: false

agi_mean, agi_median = agi["AGI"].mean(), agi["AGI"].median()
agi_above = 100 * (agi["AGI"] > agi_mean).mean()
```

The mean household AGI is `{python} money(agi_mean*10000)` and the median is
`{python} money(agi_median*10000)`. Only
`{python} f"{agi_above:.1f}"`% of households earn more than the *average*
household.

::: {.scarlet}
This is the shape of nearly every income distribution ever measured, and it is
why "average income" is a number to distrust in a policy argument. If you are
building a case about typical households, the median is the honest statistic
and you should say which one you used.
:::

::: {.brown}
Two notes on this data set, both of which you would want stated if you were
the reader rather than the writer.

First, these observations are **simulated** from the counts the IRS publishes
by zip code — the IRS does not release household-level returns. The shape is
real; no individual row is a real household.

Second, this file is a random sample of `{python} num(len(agi))` households
drawn from roughly 1.3 million. Sampling is Chapter 7's subject, and the
reason a sample this size is safe here is exactly what that chapter is about.
:::

## Which measure should you use?

|  | Advantage | Disadvantage |
|---|---|---|
| **Mean** | Easy to compute and to explain; uses every observation | Pulled by outliers |
| **Median** | Unaffected by outliers | Ignores the size of the values on either side |
| **Mode** | The only option for categorical data | May not exist, and may not be unique |

::: {.charcoal}
The practical rule: report both the mean and the median. When they agree,
you have lost nothing. When they disagree, you have found the most important
sentence in your write-up.
:::

## Doing this in Excel

Many of you will present this work in Excel, and the formulas are direct:

| Statistic | Excel |
|---|---|
| Mean | `=AVERAGE(range)` |
| Median | `=MEDIAN(range)` |
| Mode | `=MODE.SNGL(range)` |
| Weighted mean | `=SUMPRODUCT(values, weights)/SUM(weights)` |
| Standard deviation (sample) | `=STDEV.S(range)` |
| Variance (sample) | `=VAR.S(range)` |
| Percentile | `=PERCENTILE.EXC(range, k)` |
| Percentile rank | `=PERCENTRANK.EXC(range, value)` |
| Quartile | `=QUARTILE.EXC(range, quart)` |
| Correlation | `=CORREL(range1, range2)` |

Excel's **Data Analysis** add-in produces the whole descriptive block at once:
**Data → Data Analysis → Descriptive Statistics**, tick *Summary statistics*.
If the Data Analysis button is not on your ribbon, it is an add-in you enable
under **File → Options → Add-ins → Analysis ToolPak**.

You do not have to build the workbook by hand:

::: {.prompt}
Prompt

> Using `data/grad_student_gpa.csv` from
> <https://github.com/jcrooker/mba775>, build an Excel workbook with two
> sheets. Sheet 1 holds the raw GPA data. Sheet 2 computes the mean, median,
> mode, sample standard deviation, sample variance, minimum, maximum, range,
> and the first and third quartiles — each with a real Excel formula
> referencing Sheet 1, not a pasted value, so I can change the data and watch
> the summary update. Label every row. Give me the file to download.
:::

::: {.charcoal}
`PERCENTILE.EXC` and `PERCENTILE.INC` are different functions and give
different answers. This course uses the `.EXC` form, which matches the index
point rule defined below. If your number disagrees with a classmate's in the
fourth decimal place, this is usually why — and being able to say *which* rule
produced your number is the actual skill.
:::

# Measures of Variability

Two data sets can share a mean and have nothing else in common. Variability is
what separates them.

## The Range

::: {.blue}
The **range** is the largest value minus the smallest value.
:::

### Example: annual returns to the S&P 500

```{python}
#| label: sp-bar
_ = returns_bar(returns["year"], returns["sp500"],
                title="Annual return, S&P 500",
                xlab="Year", ylab="Return")
```

```{python}
#| label: sp-summary
describe(returns["sp500"], name="S&P 500 annual return").to_frame()
```

```{python}
#| label: sp-range
#| include: false

sp = returns["sp500"].dropna()
sp_range = sp.max() - sp.min()
best = returns.loc[returns["sp500"].idxmax()]
worst = returns.loc[returns["sp500"].idxmin()]
n_years = len(sp)
```

Over these `{python} str(n_years)` years the range is
`{python} f"{sp_range:.4f}"` — `{python} f"{100*sp_range:.1f}"` percentage
points separating the best year (`{python} str(int(best['year']))`, at
`{python} f"{100*best['sp500']:+.1f}"`%) from the worst
(`{python} str(int(worst['year']))`, at
`{python} f"{100*worst['sp500']:+.1f}"`%).

::: {.brown}
The range is built from exactly two observations and ignores the other
`{python} str(n_years - 2)`. Add one catastrophic year and the range moves;
add fifty ordinary years and it does not move at all. It is a useful headline
and a poor summary.
:::

## The Variance and the Standard Deviation

::: {.blue}
For a *sample*, the **variance** is

$$\hat{\sigma}^2=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(x_i-\bar{x}\right)^2.$$

The **standard deviation** is its square root:

$$\hat{\sigma}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(x_i-\bar{x}\right)^2}.$$
:::

The standard deviation is carried in the same units as the original data — the
variance is in units *squared*, which is why nobody reports "the variance in
returns was 0.0246 return-squared." Square it back and report the standard
deviation.

::: {.brown}
The divisor is $n-1$, not $n$. The sample variance computed this way is an
**unbiased estimator** of the population variance: repeat the sampling many
times and the average of the sample variances converges on the true value.
Divide by $n$ and you will, on average, understate the spread.

In Excel this is the difference between `STDEV.S` and `STDEV.P`. In pandas it
is the `ddof` argument, and pandas defaults to the sample version while numpy
defaults to the population version. Two libraries in the same language, two
different answers. Know which one you called.
:::

```{python}
#| label: ddof-demo
s = returns["sp500"].dropna()
pd.DataFrame({
    "divisor": ["n - 1  (sample, Excel STDEV.S)", "n      (population, STDEV.P)"],
    "standard deviation": [round(s.std(ddof=1), 6), round(s.std(ddof=0), 6)],
})
```

# Using the Mean and Standard Deviation Together

## The Coefficient of Variation

::: {.brown}
The **coefficient of variation** measures the standard deviation as a
percentage of the mean:

$$CV=\frac{\hat{\sigma}}{\bar{x}}\cdot100.$$
:::

### Example: the S&P 500 against Walmart

```{python}
#| label: wmt-bar
_ = returns_bar(returns["year"], returns["wmt"],
                title="Annual return, Walmart",
                xlab="Year", ylab="Return")
```

```{python}
#| label: cv-table
cv_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "S&P 500": describe(returns["sp500"]),
    "Walmart": describe(returns["wmt"]),
})
cv_table.loc[["n", "mean", "median", "std_dev", "range", "CV_percent"]].round(4)
```

```{python}
#| label: cv-stats
#| include: false

sp_v = returns["sp500"].dropna()
wm_v = returns["wmt"].dropna()
sp_sd, wm_sd = sp_v.std(ddof=1), wm_v.std(ddof=1)
sp_mu, wm_mu = sp_v.mean(), wm_v.mean()
sp_cv = coefficient_of_variation(sp_v)
wm_cv = coefficient_of_variation(wm_v)
sd_ratio = wm_sd / sp_sd
riskier_by_sd = "Walmart" if wm_sd > sp_sd else "the S&P 500"
riskier_by_cv = "Walmart" if wm_cv > sp_cv else "the S&P 500"
```

Written out for each:

```{python}
#| label: cv-math
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
show_math(rf"CV_{{S\&P}}=\frac{{{sp_sd:.4f}}}{{{sp_mu:.4f}}}\cdot100={sp_cv:.1f}")
show_math(rf"CV_{{WMT}}=\frac{{{wm_sd:.4f}}}{{{wm_mu:.4f}}}\cdot100={wm_cv:.1f}")
```

::: {.scarlet}
Read those two lines together.

Walmart's standard deviation is `{python} f"{sd_ratio:.2f}"` times the S&P
500's, so by standard deviation alone `{python} riskier_by_sd` is the more
volatile holding — and that is true. But Walmart's *coefficient of variation*
is `{python} f"{wm_cv:.1f}"` against the index's
`{python} f"{sp_cv:.1f}"`, because the mean return it is deviating around is
`{python} f"{wm_mu/sp_mu:.1f}"` times larger. Per unit of return earned,
`{python} riskier_by_cv` carried the more variable ride.

An MBA who takes only the standard deviation away from this chapter will rank
those two backwards. The standard deviation answers *"how much does it move?"*
The coefficient of variation answers *"how much does it move, given what it
pays?"* — and the second question is the one an investment committee is
actually asking.
:::

::: {.brown}
The coefficient of variation is only interpretable when the mean is positive
and comfortably away from zero. As $\bar{x}$ approaches zero the ratio
explodes, and for a mean that can be negative — a spread, a net change, a
margin swing — the CV is meaningless and occasionally sign-flipped. Check the
mean before you quote the ratio.
:::

## The $z$-score

::: {.brown}
The **$z$-score** is the number of standard deviations a particular value sits
from the mean of its distribution:

$$z=\frac{x-\bar{x}}{\hat{\sigma}}.$$

Values with $|z|>3$ are conventionally categorised as **outliers**.
:::

Expressing a value as a $z$-score is what makes two things measured in
different units comparable at all. It is also the machinery underneath every
inference test in the second half of this course, so it repays attention now.

### Example: $z$-scores and inflation

```{python}
#| label: cpi-hist
_ = histogram(cpi["inflation"].dropna(), bins=30,
              title="US inflation rate, 12-month log change in CPI",
              xlab="Inflation rate", ylab="Months")
```

```{python}
#| label: cpi-summary
describe(cpi["inflation"], name="12-month inflation").to_frame()
```

```{python}
#| label: cpi-peak
#| include: false

infl = cpi.dropna(subset=["inflation"]).copy()
mu_i, sd_i = infl["inflation"].mean(), infl["inflation"].std(ddof=1)
peak = infl.loc[infl["inflation"].idxmax()]
z_peak = z_score(peak["inflation"], mu_i, sd_i)
n_higher = int((infl["inflation"] > peak["inflation"]).sum())
recent = infl.iloc[-1]
z_recent = z_score(recent["inflation"], mu_i, sd_i)
peak_label = f"{peak['date']:%B %Y}"
recent_label = f"{recent['date']:%B %Y}"
outlier_word = "does" if abs(z_peak) > 3 else "does not"
```

The highest 12-month inflation rate in this series is
`{python} f"{100*peak['inflation']:.2f}"`%, in `{python} peak_label`. Its
$z$-score is

```{python}
#| label: cpi-z-math
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
show_math(r"z=\frac{x-\bar{x}}{\hat{\sigma}}"
          rf"=\frac{{{peak['inflation']:.4f}-{mu_i:.4f}}}{{{sd_i:.4f}}}"
          rf"={z_peak:.4f}")
```

That month sits `{python} f"{z_peak:.2f}"` standard deviations above the
average month, and `{python} outlier_word` clear the conventional $|z|>3$
threshold for an outlier.

The most recent observation, `{python} recent_label`, sits at
`{python} f"{100*recent['inflation']:.2f}"`% — a $z$-score of
`{python} f"{z_recent:.2f}"`. Two inflation rates, the same units, and the
$z$-score is what lets you say how far apart they really are.

### How unusual is unusual?

A $z$-score is only useful if you can turn it back into a count. Here is every
month whose inflation rate was more than two standard deviations above the
mean:

```{python}
#| label: cpi-extremes
threshold = mu_i + 2 * sd_i
extreme = infl[infl["inflation"] > threshold]
print(f"Threshold (z = 2): {100*threshold:.2f}% inflation")
print(f"Months above it:   {len(extreme):,} of {len(infl):,} "
      f"({100*len(extreme)/len(infl):.2f}%)")
print()
print(extreme.assign(month=extreme["date"].dt.strftime("%b %Y"),
                     inflation_pct=(100*extreme["inflation"]).round(2))
             .nlargest(8, "inflation")[["month", "inflation_pct"]]
             .to_string(index=False))
```

```{python}
#| label: cpi-series
_ = time_series(cpi["date"], cpi["inflation"],
                title="US inflation rate, 12-month log change in CPI",
                ylab="Inflation rate")
```

## The Empirical Rule

::: {.brown}
If a distribution is bell-shaped and symmetric, approximately 68%, 95%, and
99.7% of the values fall within one, two, and three standard deviations of the
mean, respectively.

Rearranged, a value can be recovered from its $z$-score:

$$x=\mu+\sigma\cdot z.$$
:::

```{python}
#| label: bell
_ = normal_curve()
```

That picture is of a mathematical function, not of any data set. The rule only
applies to the extent your data resembles it, and that is a claim to be
checked rather than assumed:

```{python}
#| label: empirical-check
empirical_rule(unrate["unemployment_rate"], name="UNRATE")
```

```{python}
#| label: empirical-check-agi
empirical_rule(agi["AGI"], name="Nevada AGI")
```

```{python}
#| label: empirical-compare
#| include: false

er_u = empirical_rule(unrate["unemployment_rate"])
er_a = empirical_rule(agi["AGI"])
u1 = er_u.loc["1 sd", "actual_percent"]
a1 = er_a.loc["1 sd", "actual_percent"]
a_low3 = er_a.loc["3 sd", "interval_low"]
```

For the unemployment rate, `{python} f"{u1:.1f}"`% of months fall within one
standard deviation of the mean, against the 68.3% the bell curve predicts.
For Nevada AGI the figure is `{python} f"{a1:.1f}"`%.

::: {.scarlet}
Look at the `interval_low` column of the AGI table. Three standard deviations
below the mean is `{python} f"{a_low3:.2f}"` — a *negative* income, in a data
set where nothing can be below zero. The empirical rule did not fail here; it
was never applicable. Applying a symmetric rule to a skewed distribution
produces intervals that reach into territory the variable cannot occupy, and
nothing in the arithmetic warns you.
:::

## Chebyshev's Theorem

::: {.blue}
**Chebyshev's Theorem** states that for any $z>1$, the percentage of values
falling within $z$ standard deviations of the mean is at least

$$\left(1-\frac{1}{z^2}\right)\cdot100.$$
:::

This is the tool for the situation you are actually in most of the time: a
distribution whose shape you do not know. It applies to *every* distribution —
skewed, bimodal, lumpy, anything — which is exactly why the guarantee it gives
is weak. It is a floor, never an estimate.

### Applied to inflation

Take the two standard deviation threshold from the section above. What does
Chebyshev guarantee about how often inflation can exceed it?

```{python}
#| label: cheb-cpi
chebyshev_table(2).to_frame("Chebyshev at z = 2")
```

```{python}
#| label: cheb-cpi-math
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
show_math(r"\left(1-\frac{1}{z^2}\right)\cdot100"
          rf"=\left(1-\frac{{1}}{{(2)^2}}\right)\cdot100={chebyshev(2):.2f}")
```

```{python}
#| label: cheb-cpi-values
#| include: false

cheb_in = chebyshev(2)
cheb_out = 100 - cheb_in
cheb_tail = cheb_out / 2
actual_in = float(((infl["inflation"] >= mu_i - 2*sd_i) &
                   (infl["inflation"] <= mu_i + 2*sd_i)).mean() * 100)
actual_tail = 100 * len(infl[infl["inflation"] > mu_i + 2*sd_i]) / len(infl)
```

At least `{python} f"{cheb_in:.2f}"`% of months must lie within two standard
deviations of the mean, so at most `{python} f"{cheb_out:.2f}"`% lie outside
that interval — and, if we are willing to treat the two tails as comparable,
at most `{python} f"{cheb_tail:.2f}"`% above it.

In this data, `{python} f"{actual_in:.2f}"`% of months actually fell inside
that interval and `{python} f"{actual_tail:.2f}"`% were above it.

::: {.charcoal}
The bound held, and it held by a wide margin. That is the normal outcome and
it is the thing to understand about Chebyshev: it is almost always loose. It
tells you what *cannot* be true, not what is likely. A consultant who reports
the Chebyshev bound as a forecast has reported a number that is correct and
useless at the same time.

Two cautions worth carrying out of here. The theorem bounds both tails
together; splitting the remainder in half assumes a symmetry the theorem never
promised, so state a one-tail figure as an upper bound and never as an
estimate. And for $z \le 1$ the formula returns zero or worse — it tells you
nothing at all, which is honest but unquotable.
:::

### Applied to graduate GPA

```{python}
#| label: gpa-cheb-stats
#| include: false

gpa_mu = gpa["GPA"].mean()
gpa_sd = gpa["GPA"].std(ddof=1)
z_gpa = z_score(3.0, gpa_mu, gpa_sd)
gpa_in = chebyshev(z_gpa)
gpa_tail = (100 - gpa_in) / 2
gpa_actual = 100 * (gpa["GPA"] < 3.0).mean()
```

What fraction of graduate students should we expect to hold a GPA below 3.0?
The $z$-score of a 3.0 is

```{python}
#| label: gpa-z-math
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
show_math(rf"z=\frac{{3.0-{gpa_mu:.4f}}}{{{gpa_sd:.4f}}}={z_gpa:.4f}")
```

```{python}
#| label: cheb-gpa
chebyshev_table(z_gpa).to_frame("Chebyshev for a 3.0 GPA")
```

```{python}
#| label: gpa-actual
print(f"Students below a 3.0 GPA: {int((gpa['GPA'] < 3.0).sum())} "
      f"of {len(gpa)}  ({gpa_actual:.2f}%)")
```

Chebyshev bounds the share below 3.0 at no more than
`{python} f"{gpa_tail:.2f}"`%. The actual figure is
`{python} f"{gpa_actual:.2f}"`%.

::: {.brown}
Note how far apart those two numbers are, and note the direction: the bound is
not close, but it is not violated either. That is what a guarantee that holds
for *any* distribution costs you. If you are willing to assume a shape, you
can say far more — which is what Chapters 5 and 6 are for.
:::

# Working with Grouped Data

Sometimes you never see the individual observations. What you are handed is a
table of counts by class, which is how most published statistics arrive.

::: {.blue}
The **midpoint** of a class is the average of its endpoints.

The **sample mean for grouped data** is

$$\bar{x}\approx\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{k}f_i\cdot m_i,$$

where $f_i$ is the frequency of class $i$, $m_i$ its midpoint,
$n=\sum_{i=1}^{k}f_i$, and $k$ the number of classes.

The **sample variance for grouped data** is

$$\hat{\sigma}^2=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^{k}f_i\cdot\left(m_i-\bar{x}\right)^2.$$
:::

## Application: adjusted gross income in zip code 89015

The IRS publishes tax return counts by zip code and income bracket at its
[SOI zip code data portal](https://www.irs.gov/statistics/soi-tax-stats-individual-income-tax-statistics-zip-code-data-soi).
Below are the 2016 counts for zip code 89015 — Henderson, Nevada.

```{python}
#| label: grouped-input
# IRS SOI, tax year 2016, zip code 89015. Counts of returns by AGI bracket.
brackets = pd.DataFrame({
    "class":     ["$1 - $25,000", "$25,000 - $50,000", "$50,000 - $75,000",
                  "$75,000 - $100,000", "$100,000 - $200,000",
                  "$200,000 - $300,000"],
    "low":       [1, 25_000, 50_000, 75_000, 100_000, 200_000],
    "high":      [25_000, 50_000, 75_000, 100_000, 200_000, 300_000],
    "frequency": [6_600, 4_820, 2_550, 1_600, 1_790, 310],
})
brackets["midpoint"] = (brackets["low"] + brackets["high"]) / 2
brackets
```

```{python}
#| label: grouped-work
work = grouped_summary(brackets["frequency"], brackets["midpoint"],
                       labels=brackets["class"])
work.style.format({"frequency_f": "{:,.0f}", "midpoint_m": "{:,.2f}",
                   "f_times_m": "{:,.2f}", "deviation": "{:,.2f}",
                   "f_times_dev_sq": "{:,.2f}"}, na_rep="")
```

```{python}
#| label: grouped-stats
#| include: false

g_n = int(brackets["frequency"].sum())
g_mean = grouped_mean(brackets["frequency"], brackets["midpoint"])
g_var = grouped_variance(brackets["frequency"], brackets["midpoint"])
g_sd = np.sqrt(g_var)
g_fm = float((brackets["frequency"] * brackets["midpoint"]).sum())
g_fd = float((brackets["frequency"] *
              (brackets["midpoint"] - g_mean) ** 2).sum())
```

Reading the totals off that table:

```{python}
#| label: grouped-math
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
show_math(rf"\bar{{x}}=\frac{{1}}{{{mnum(g_n)}}}"
          rf"\left[{mnum(g_fm)}\right]={mmoney(g_mean, 2)}")
show_math(rf"\hat{{\sigma}}^2=\frac{{1}}{{{mnum(g_n-1)}}}"
          rf"\left[{mnum(g_fd)}\right]={mnum(g_var, 2)}")
show_math(rf"\hat{{\sigma}}=\sqrt{{{mnum(g_var, 2)}}}={mmoney(g_sd, 2)}")
```

::: {.brown}
Every observation inside a class has been replaced by that class's midpoint,
so this is an approximation and the note should say so. The top class is the
worst offender: "\$200,000 – \$300,000" gets a midpoint of \$250,000, and if
the published table's top class had been open-ended — "\$200,000 or more" — you
would have to invent a midpoint, and your standard deviation would inherit
whatever you invented.
:::

### What share earns above \$250,000?

We do not know the shape of this distribution, so Chebyshev is the only tool
available.

```{python}
#| label: grouped-z-math
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
z_agi = z_score(250_000, g_mean, g_sd)
show_math(rf"z=\frac{{{mnum(250000)}-{mnum(g_mean, 2)}}}{{{mnum(g_sd, 2)}}}"
          rf"={z_agi:.4f}")
```

```{python}
#| label: grouped-cheb
chebyshev_table(z_agi).to_frame("Chebyshev at $250,000")
```

```{python}
#| label: grouped-cheb-stats
#| include: false

zagi_in = chebyshev(z_agi)
zagi_tail = (100 - zagi_in) / 2
```

At least `{python} f"{zagi_in:.2f}"`% of this zip code's returns fall within
`{python} f"{z_agi:.2f}"` standard deviations of the mean, so no more than
`{python} f"{zagi_tail:.2f}"`% report AGI above \$250,000.

::: {.charcoal}
Check that against the table you started from: the published counts say
`{python} num(brackets['frequency'].iloc[-1])` of `{python} num(g_n)` returns
— `{python} f"{100*brackets['frequency'].iloc[-1]/g_n:.2f}"`% — fall in the
top bracket at all. The bound is true and the bound is loose. When you have
the counts, count. Chebyshev is for when you do not.
:::

# Measures of Relative Position

Where does one value sit relative to the rest?

::: {.blue}
A **percentile** measures the approximate percentage of values in the data set
that fall below the value of interest.

The **$\rho$th percentile** is the value that at least $\rho$ percent of the
observations fall below.

The **index point** for the $p$th percentile is

$$i=\frac{p}{100}\cdot n.$$

If $i$ is not a whole number, round up; that position holds the value. If $i$
is a whole number, take the midpoint of positions $i$ and $i+1$.
:::

```{python}
#| label: pct-80
percentile(gpa["GPA"], 0.80)
```

```{python}
#| label: pct-80-stats
#| include: false

p80 = percentile(gpa["GPA"], 0.80)
p80_i = 0.80 * len(gpa)
```

With $n=`{python} num(len(gpa))`$ students, the index point for the 80th
percentile is $0.80 \times `{python} num(len(gpa))` = `{python} num(p80_i, 1)`$.
The 80th percentile GPA is `{python} f"{p80:.4f}"`.

::: {.charcoal}
There is more than one rule for this, and different software uses different
ones. Here is the same percentile computed three ways:
:::

```{python}
#| label: pct-methods
percentile_methods(gpa["GPA"], 0.80).to_frame()
```

They are close, and on a data set this size the disagreement is in the third
decimal. On a data set of twelve observations it would not be. This course
uses the index-point rule above, matching Excel's `PERCENTILE.EXC`. The point
is not that one is right — it is that you should be able to say which rule
produced your number when someone else's differs.

## Percentile rank

::: {.blue}
The **percentile rank** of a value $x$ is

$$\text{Percentile Rank}=\frac{1}{n}\left[\frac{1}{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}I\{x_i<x\}\right]\cdot100,$$

where $I\{\cdot\}$ is an **indicator function** taking the value 1 when the
statement inside is true and 0 when it is false.
:::

```{python}
#| label: pct-rank
round(percentile_rank(gpa["GPA"], 3.75), 2)
```

```{python}
#| label: pct-rank-stats
#| include: false

pr = percentile_rank(gpa["GPA"], 3.75)
n_below = int((gpa["GPA"] < 3.75).sum())
```

A student with a 3.75 GPA sits at the `{python} f"{pr:.2f}"`th percentile:
`{python} num(n_below)` of `{python} num(len(gpa))` students are below them.

Percentile and percentile rank are inverses of one another. The first takes a
percentage and returns a value; the second takes a value and returns a
percentage. Getting them the wrong way round is the most common error in this
section.

## Quartiles and the interquartile range

::: {.blue}
The first, second, and third **quartiles** are the 25th, 50th, and 75th
percentiles. The second quartile is the median.

The **interquartile range** is

$$IQR=Q_3-Q_1,$$

the spread of the middle 50% of the data.
:::

```{python}
#| label: quartiles
q1, q2, q3 = quartiles(gpa["GPA"])
lo, hi = outlier_fences(gpa["GPA"])
pd.Series({
    "Q1 (25th percentile)": q1,
    "Q2 (median)": q2,
    "Q3 (75th percentile)": q3,
    "IQR": q3 - q1,
    "lower fence  Q1 - 1.5*IQR": lo,
    "upper fence  Q3 + 1.5*IQR": hi,
}).round(4).to_frame("Graduate GPA")
```

The IQR is a measure of spread with the same virtue the median has: the two
most extreme observations in the data set cannot move it. Where the range is
built entirely from outliers, the IQR is immune to them.

## Box-and-whisker plots

The box runs from $Q_1$ to $Q_3$ with the median marked inside it, so the box
*is* the interquartile range drawn to scale. The whiskers extend to the most
extreme observations still within $Q_1-1.5\cdot IQR$ and $Q_3+1.5\cdot IQR$.
Anything beyond those fences is plotted individually and is what this chapter
means by an outlier.

```{python}
#| label: gpa-box
_ = box_plot(gpa["GPA"], title="Graduate student GPA", xlab="GPA")
```

The long lower whisker and the short upper one are the left skew, seen from a
different angle. The diamond marks the mean; that it sits below the median
line is the same fact the histogram showed.

Box plots earn their keep when comparing groups:

```{python}
#| label: returns-box
_ = box_plot([returns["sp500"].dropna(), returns["wmt"].dropna()],
             labels=["S&P 500", "Walmart"],
             title="Annual returns over the last 50 years",
             xlab="Annual return")
```

## The five-number summary

::: {.blue}
By convention, five statistics describe a data set and the shape of its
distribution: the **minimum**, the **first quartile**, the **median**, the
**third quartile**, and the **maximum**.
:::

```{python}
#| label: five-number
pd.DataFrame({
    "Graduate GPA": five_number_summary(gpa["GPA"]),
    "S&P 500 return": five_number_summary(returns["sp500"]),
    "Walmart return": five_number_summary(returns["wmt"]),
    "Unemployment rate": five_number_summary(unrate["unemployment_rate"]),
})
```

That is the box plot as a table, and it is the block Excel produces from
**Data → Data Analysis → Descriptive Statistics**.

# Measures of Association Between Two Variables

::: {.blue}
The **sample covariance** measures the *direction* of the linear relationship
between two variables:

$$\hat{\sigma}_{xy}=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(x_i-\bar{x}\right)\left(y_i-\bar{y}\right).$$
:::

::: {.blue}
The **sample correlation coefficient** measures both the strength and the
direction:

$$\hat{\rho}_{xy}=\frac{\hat{\sigma}_{xy}}{\hat{\sigma}_x\hat{\sigma}_y},$$

where $\hat{\sigma}_x$ and $\hat{\sigma}_y$ are the sample standard deviations
of $x$ and $y$. It always lies between $-1$ and $+1$.
:::

```{python}
#| label: assoc-scatter
paired = returns.dropna(subset=["sp500", "wmt"])
_ = scatter(paired["sp500"], paired["wmt"],
            title="Annual returns: Walmart against the S&P 500",
            xlab="S&P 500 annual return", ylab="Walmart annual return")
```

```{python}
#| label: assoc-returns
association(paired["sp500"], paired["wmt"], "sp500", "wmt") \
    .round(6).to_frame("S&P 500 vs Walmart")
```

```{python}
#| label: assoc-stats
#| include: false

a_ret = association(paired["sp500"], paired["wmt"], "sp500", "wmt")
cov_ret = a_ret["covariance"]
cor_ret = a_ret["correlation"]
direction = "move together" if cov_ret > 0 else "move in opposite directions"
strength = ("weak" if abs(cor_ret) < 0.3 else
            "moderate" if abs(cor_ret) < 0.6 else "strong")
```

The covariance is `{python} f"{cov_ret:.6f}"`. Its sign says the two
`{python} direction`. Its magnitude says nothing you can act on, because it
carries the units of both variables multiplied together — rescale returns from
decimals to percentages and the covariance changes by a factor of 10,000 while
the relationship does not change at all.

Dividing by both standard deviations removes the units and leaves
`{python} f"{cor_ret:.4f}"` — a `{python} strength` positive relationship, on a
scale that runs from $-1$ to $+1$ and means the same thing whatever the
variables were measured in.

```{python}
#| label: assoc-states
state_pairs = states[["HPI", "UR", "POPN", "gPOP"]].dropna()
state_pairs.corr().round(3)
```

::: {.scarlet}
A correlation matrix is the fastest way to mislead yourself in this entire
course. Four things it does not tell you:

1. **Causation.** Neither direction, nor the possibility that a third variable
   drives both.
2. **Non-linear relationships.** A perfect U-shape can produce a correlation
   of zero. Draw the scatter plot before you trust the coefficient.
3. **What outliers did to it.** A single extreme pair can create a correlation
   or destroy one, and the number gives no hint.
4. **Whether the sample is large enough to mean anything.** With
   `{python} num(len(state_pairs))` observations, a coefficient of 0.25 is
   not distinguishable from zero — which is a Chapter 9 question, and one we
   will come back to.
:::

> sheets. Sheet 1 holds the raw annual returns for the S&P 500 and Walmart.
> Sheet 2 computes, for each series, the mean, median, sample standard
> deviation, minimum, maximum, range, and coefficient of variation, plus the
> correlation between the two series — every cell a real Excel formula
> referencing Sheet 1, not a pasted value. Add a column chart of both return

When it opens, change one year's return to something extreme and watch which
statistics move and which do not. The ones that barely move are the resistant
ones, and now you know why.
